title: Sodium Hydroxide and Sodium Carbonate
topicTitle: Sodium hydroxide: properties and uses; sodium carbonate: properties, action with CO2, SO2, water, precipitation reactions and uses
notes: **Chlor-alkali process (NaOH production):** The most important industrial process for sodium hydroxide. Electrolysis of aqueous NaCl (brine) produces NaOH, Cl₂, and H₂. Three cell types exist: (1) Mercury cell: Na amalgam forms at Hg cathode, then reacts with water: Na(Hg) + H₂O → NaOH + ½H₂ + Hg. Produces 50% NaOH but mercury pollution is a concern. (2) Diaphragm cell: asbestos/cation-exchange diaphragm separates anode and cathode. Produces ~10% NaOH requiring concentration. (3) Membrane cell: modern ion-exchange membrane (Nafion) produces 30–35% NaOH with high purity. Global NaOH production: 80+ million tonnes/year.

**NaOH (caustic soda) — properties:** White, odourless, crystalline solid (mp = 318°C, bp = 1388°C). Extremely hygroscopic — absorbs moisture from air (deliquescent) and CO₂ to form Na₂CO₃. Very soluble in water (100 g/100 mL at 20°C) with vigorous exothermic dissolution (ΔH = −44.5 kJ/mol). Strong base (pKb = −0.6), fully dissociates in water: NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻. Corrosive to organic tissue — causes severe chemical burns by saponifying fats in skin.

**NaOH reactions — with amphoteric metals:** NaOH dissolves aluminium and zinc with hydrogen evolution: 2Al + 2NaOH + 6H₂O → 2Na[Al(OH)₄] + 3H₂ (sodium aluminate formed) or Al + NaOH + 3H₂O → Na[Al(OH)₄] + ¾H₂. Similarly: Zn + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂. These reactions demonstrate the amphoteric nature of Al and Zn — their oxides/hydroxides dissolve in both acids and bases. This property is exploited in the Bayer process for aluminium extraction.

**NaOH reactions — with non-metals:** (1) With Cl₂ (cold, dilute): Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaOCl + H₂O (bleaching powder precursor). (2) With Cl₂ (hot, concentrated): 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O (sodium chlorate formation). (3) With S: 16NaOH + 3S → 2Na₂S + Na₂S₂O₃ + 8H₂O. (4) With CO₂: 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O (this is why NaOH solutions must be stored in sealed containers — they absorb atmospheric CO₂).

**Precipitation reactions of NaOH:** NaOH forms characteristic precipitates with metal ions, useful in qualitative analysis: (1) Cu²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Cu(OH)₂↓ (blue precipitate, soluble in excess NH₃ but NOT in excess NaOH — distinguishes from Zn²⁺). (2) Fe²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₂↓ (green precipitate, turns brown Fe(OH)₃ on standing). (3) Fe³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₃↓ (reddish-brown precipitate, insoluble in excess NaOH). (4) Al³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → Al(OH)₃↓ (white precipitate, DISSOLVES in excess NaOH forming [Al(OH)₄]⁻ — amphoteric). (5) Zn²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Zn(OH)₂↓ (white precipitate, DISSOLVES in excess NaOH forming [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻).

**Solvay process (ammonia-soda process):** The primary industrial method for Na₂CO₃ production (100+ million tonnes/year globally). Invented by Ernest Solvay in 1861. Key reactions: (1) NH₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → NH₄HCO₃ (carbonation tower). (2) NH₄HCO₃ + NaCl → NaHCO₃↓ + NH₄Cl (precipitation of sodium bicarbonate). (3) 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ (calcination at 150–200°C). The NH₃ is recycled. Key advantage: uses cheap NaCl and limestone (CaCO₃ → CO₂ + CaO) as raw materials.

**Sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃) — properties:** White crystalline solid, also known as washing soda (decahydrate Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) or soda ash (anhydrous). Soluble in water, hydrolyzes to give alkaline solution: CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ (pH ≈ 11.6 for 0.1 M solution). The decahydrate effloresces (loses water of crystallization) in dry air, forming the monohydrate (Na₂CO₃·H₂O). Thermal stability: anhydrous Na₂CO₃ does not decompose on heating (unlike NaHCO₃ which decomposes at 270°C).

**Action of Na₂CO₃ with CO₂:** Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ → 2NaHCO₃ (sodium bicarbonate). This reaction is the basis of the Solvay process. The solubility of NaHCO₃ (9.6 g/100 mL at 20°C) is much lower than Na₂CO₃ (21.5 g/100 mL), so NaHCO₃ precipitates out. This precipitation drives the reaction forward (Le Chatelier's principle). In nature, this reaction occurs when sodium carbonate-rich brines are exposed to atmospheric CO₂, forming bicarbonate deposits.

**Action of Na₂CO₃ with SO₂:** Na₂CO₃ + SO₂ → Na₂SO₃ + CO₂ (at moderate temperatures). This reaction is the basis of flue gas desulphurization (FGD) — removing SO₂ from industrial exhaust gases. The sodium sulphite can be oxidized to sodium sulphate: Na₂SO₃ + ½O₂ → Na₂SO₄. Alternatively, calcium-based FGD (limestone scrubbers) is more common: CaCO₃ + SO₂ → CaSO₃ + CO₂. Both methods reduce acid rain formation.

**Sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃) — baking soda:** White crystalline solid, weakly alkaline (pH ≈ 8.3). Thermally decomposes: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ at 270°C. The CO₂ released causes dough to rise in baking (hence 'baking soda'). Reacts with acids: NaHCO�3 + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Used as an antacid (neutralizes excess stomach acid: NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂), fire extinguisher (dry chemical), and in fire blankets (releases CO₂ to smother flames).

**Precipitation reactions of Na₂CO₃:** Na₂CO₃ precipitates most metal carbonates from solution: (1) Ca²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → CaCO₃↓ (white, insoluble — basis of water hardness testing). (2) Ba²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → BaCO₃↓ (white). (3) 2Ag⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → Ag₂CO₃↓ (pale yellow). (4) Cu²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ + H₂O → CuCO₃·Cu(OH)₂↓ (green basic carbonate). (5) Fe³⁺ + CO₃²⁻ + H₂O → Fe(OH)₃↓ + CO₂ (reddish-brown, because Fe³⁺ hydrolyzes carbonate). (6) Zn²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → ZnCO₃↓ (white).

**Uses of NaOH:** (1) Soap industry — saponification of fats/oils: Fat + 3NaOH → Glycerol + 3R-COONa (soap). (2) Paper industry — Kraft process uses NaOH/Na₂S to digest wood chips. (3) Aluminium production — Bayer process: Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O. (4) Textile industry — mercerization of cotton (treatment with NaOH increases luster and strength). (5) Petroleum refining — removal of acidic impurities (H₂S, mercaptans). (6) Drain cleaner — dissolves organic blockages by saponifying fats. (7) pH control in chemical manufacturing.

**Uses of Na₂CO₃:** (1) Glass manufacture — 30–40% of global production; Na₂CO₃ lowers the melting point of SiO₂ from 1700°C to ~1000°C: Na₂CO₃ + SiO₂ → Na₂SiO₃ + CO₂. (2) Water softening — precipitates Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ as carbonates: Ca²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → CaCO₃↓. (3) Laundry detergent — alkali builder that emulsifies grease. (4) pH regulator in swimming pools and textile dyeing. (5) Chemical synthesis — precursor to other sodium compounds (NaHCO₃, Na₂S, Na₃PO₄). (6) Food industry — pasta maker, chocolate processing, olive curing.

**Environmental and health considerations:** NaOH is classified as a severe skin corrosive (GHS Category 1). Eye contact can cause permanent blindness. Na₂CO₃ is less hazardous but can irritate eyes and respiratory tract. The chlor-alkali industry produces Cl₂ (toxic gas) as a co-product — modern plants must have robust containment. Mercury cell plants are being phased out globally (Minamata Convention) due to mercury pollution. Membrane cell technology is the environmental standard.
confusion: NaOH vs. Na₂CO₃ alkalinity: Both are alkaline, but NaOH is a STRONG base (fully dissociates, pH ≈ 14 for 1 M) while Na₂CO₃ is a WEAK base (hydrolyzes partially, pH ≈ 11.6 for 0.1 M). This distinction matters in applications: NaOH is used for aggressive cleaning (drain cleaner, saponification), while Na₂CO₃ is used for gentler applications (water softening, food processing). Confusing them can lead to dangerous over-concentration of NaOH in cleaning products.

Na₂CO₃·10H₂O vs. anhydrous Na₂CO₃: Washing soda is the DECAHYDRATE (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O), not the anhydrous form. When exposed to dry air, the decahydrate effloresces (loses water) to form the monohydrate (Na₂CO₃·H₂O, soda ash). The anhydrous form (soda ash) is the industrial product from the Solvay process. Students often confuse the hydrated form (used in households) with the anhydrous form (used in industry).

Why NaHCO₃ precipitates in Solvay process: The solubility of NaHCO₃ (9.6 g/100 mL) is significantly lower than Na₂CO₃ (21.5 g/100 mL) and NH₄HCO₃ (23.3 g/100 mL). When NH₄HCO₃ is mixed with concentrated NaCl, the double displacement produces NaHCO₃, which precipitates because its solubility is exceeded. The other possible product, NH₄Cl (37.2 g/100 mL), remains in solution. This solubility difference is the key to the entire process.

NaOH does NOT dissolve Al(OH)₃ because it is a base — it dissolves because Al(OH)₃ is AMPHOTERIC: Al(OH)₃ + NaOH → Na[Al(OH)₄]. The aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess NaOH because it can act as an acid (donating H⁺ to form [Al(OH)₄]⁻). This is different from NaOH dissolving a base like Cu(OH)₂ — Cu(OH)₂ does NOT dissolve in excess NaOH because copper(II) hydroxide is not amphoteric (it only dissolves in acids, not bases).

Bleaching powder is NOT NaOCl: Bleaching powder (CaOCl₂ or Ca(OCl)Cl) is prepared from Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂, NOT from NaOH. The reaction with NaOH produces NaOCl (sodium hypochlorite, liquid bleach), which is a different compound. Confusion arises because both are bleaching agents. CaOCl₂ is a solid used for water treatment and textile bleaching; NaOCl is a liquid solution used for household bleaching and disinfection.
practice: A 25.0 mL sample of NaOH solution is titrated with 0.1 M HCl using phenolphthalein indicator. If 32.5 mL of HCl is required to reach the endpoint, calculate the molarity of the NaOH solution. Then calculate the mass of Na₂CO₃ that would form if this NaOH sample was left open to air and absorbed 0.5 g of CO₂. (Reaction: 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O.)

Calculate the volume of CO₂ (at STP) released when 10.6 g of Na₂CO₃ reacts completely with excess dilute HCl. Then calculate the volume of 0.5 M HCl required for complete neutralization. (Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂; M(Na₂CO₃) = 106 g/mol.)

Describe the complete Solvay process for manufacturing Na₂CO₃, including all chemical equations. Calculate the theoretical mass of Na₂CO₃ produced from 100 kg of NaCl, assuming 90% yield at each step. Explain why the process requires recycled NH₃ and how the NH₃ is regenerated (NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → 2NH₃ + CaCl₂ + 2H₂O).

A water sample contains 200 ppm Ca²⁺ ions. Calculate the mass of Na₂CO₃ required to soften 1000 L of this water by precipitating all Ca²⁺ as CaCO₃. Then calculate the mass of NaOH needed to achieve the same result (using NaOH to precipitate Ca²⁺ — which is NOT possible directly, explaining why Na₂CO₃ is preferred for water softening). Explain why NaOH cannot be used for water softening.

In the chlor-alkali process using a membrane cell, calculate the mass of NaOH, Cl₂, and H₂ produced in 24 hours at a current of 100,000 A. (Faraday's law: m = MIt/nF.) If the cell operates at 3.0 V, calculate the energy consumption in kWh per kg of NaOH. Compare this with the theoretical minimum energy (ΔG for 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂ is +422 kJ/mol NaOH).
universalFacts: Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is one of the top 10 most produced inorganic chemicals globally, with annual production exceeding 80 million tonnes. Its economic importance is measured by the 'caustic index' — the ratio of NaOH + Na₂CO₃ production to population — used by industrial economists to gauge a nation's chemical industry development.

The Solvay process, invented in 1861, replaced the inefficient Leblanc process (which produced toxic HCl gas as a byproduct). The Solvay process was so successful that it dominated sodium carbonate production for over 150 years. Modern variants use ion-exchange membranes and optimize energy efficiency, but the core chemistry remains unchanged.

The reaction 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O is why NaOH solutions must be stored in sealed plastic (not glass) containers — CO₂ from air gradually converts NaOH to Na₂CO₃, reducing the effective concentration. In analytical chemistry, 'standard NaOH solutions' must be standardized against primary standards (KHP — potassium hydrogen phthalate) because they absorb CO₂ from air during preparation and use.

The Kraft process for paper manufacturing uses a 'white liquor' of NaOH and Na₂S to digest wood chips. The NaOH breaks down lignin (the 'glue' holding cellulose fibers together), while Na₂S accelerates the reaction and protects cellulose. This process produces 70% of the world's pulp. The 'smell' of a paper mill is due to reduced sulfur compounds (H₂S, methanethiol) in the recovery boiler.

Sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃) was originally obtained from the ash of burned seaweed (barilla process) and from natural deposits (trona ore in Wyoming, USA — the world's largest deposit, ~3 billion tonnes). The Solvay process made these sources obsolete. Today, trona mining in Wyoming produces ~40% of the world's sodium carbonate, with the Solvay process producing most of the rest.
